title: The young king faces his toughest challenge
summary:
Gukesh Dommaraju will defend his world title against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva after a remarkable rise that made him the youngest undisputed champion in history. Since his 2024 triumph, however, the Indian grandmaster has endured a more difficult period and slipped down the world rankings. The match therefore presents a different challenge: rediscovering his best form while facing a younger rival who arrives with strong recent results and considerable momentum. | Image: FIDE

Press release by FIDE

From prodigious talent to the youngest world champion in history, Gukesh Dommaraju has enjoyed a meteoric rise to the summit of the chess world. Now, as he prepares to defend his crown against Uzbekistan's rising star Javokhir Sindarov, the Indian prodigy faces perhaps the greatest challenge of his career: rediscovering his best form.

World champion Gukesh Dommaraju embodies ambition, determination and youthful excellence. His remarkable rise to the pinnacle of the chess world, marked by record-breaking achievements and historic milestones, is an extraordinary story of talent, perseverance and self-belief. At just 18 years of age, he achieved what generations of chess players can only dream of: becoming the youngest undisputed world champion in history.

Born on 29 May 2006 in Chennai, the same city that nurtured India's chess legend Viswanathan Anand, Gukesh showed signs of exceptional talent from an early age. Having learned the rules of chess at the age of seven, he quickly demonstrated a natural aptitude for the game, winning the Asian School Chess Championships in 2015. Soon afterwards, he left formal schooling to devote himself entirely to chess.

With the unwavering support of his parents, Gukesh continued to develop his skills, becoming an international master in 2017. His training approach placed particular emphasis on independent thinking and understanding positions rather than relying on chess engines. This helped him develop a distinctive playing style and strong analytical abilities. In January 2019, at the age of just 12 years, 7 months and 17 days, he became the second-youngest grandmaster in chess history.

Photo: John Saunders

His progress continued at an impressive pace. After collecting medals at international youth championships, Gukesh spent the Covid period further strengthening his game, and competed both online and over the board. Another breakthrough came at the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai, where he represented India's second team, helping it secure the bronze medal. Individually, he produced a spectacular performance on the first board, scoring 9 points out of 11 and winning the individual gold medal.

Further outstanding results in 2022 and 2023 propelled him into the world's elite. He became the youngest player ever to surpass the 2750 Elo rating mark and qualified for the 2024 Candidates Tournament. Held in April, this prestigious competition brought together eight of the world's strongest players to determine the challenger to reigning world champion Ding Liren. Gukesh once again made history by becoming the youngest Candidates' winner ever.

Photo: Michal Walusza

September 2024 brought another landmark achievement for Indian chess. At the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, India claimed its first-ever gold medal. Gukesh played a central role in this historic triumph, winning the individual gold medal on board one with an outstanding score of 9 points out of 10 and a stellar rating performance of 3056. This result also propelled him into the world's top five and helped him reach a new personal rating peak.

In November and December 2024, Gukesh faced Ding Liren in the World Championship match in Singapore. The contest began with a setback for the Indian, who lost the first game with the white pieces. However, he responded with remarkable composure, demonstrating the resilience and fighting spirit that had characterised his rise to the top. The match remained balanced as the two players traded blows.

Everything came down to the fourteenth and final game. In a dramatic endgame, Gukesh capitalised on a mistake from his opponent and secured victory by the narrowest of margins, 7½–6½. At just 18, he became the youngest undisputed world champion in chess history, breaking a record that Garry Kasparov had held for more than four decades.

Photo: Eng Chin An

With this extraordinary achievement, Gukesh became India's second world chess champion after Viswanathan Anand and emerged as an inspiration for a new generation of players, both at home and around the world.

Throughout his rise, Gukesh has consistently displayed a growth-oriented mindset. Even after capturing the world title, he made it clear that winning the championship was not the ultimate destination, but rather another milestone on his journey. He openly acknowledged that there was still much to learn before he could establish himself as the world's strongest player. The period that followed, however, proved considerably more challenging than expected. Having reached the pinnacle at such a remarkably young age, Gukesh appeared to encounter the first significant plateau of his career. Since around the middle of 2025, his results have been increasingly inconsistent, with a series of disappointing performances affecting his position among the world’s elite. He has since slipped to 26 th place in the FIDE rating list, with 2710 Elo points.

For a reigning world champion, such a decline inevitably raises questions about confidence, form and the ability to withstand the pressure that comes with defending the ultimate title. Gukesh now faces the difficult task of rediscovering the form that made him virtually unstoppable during his remarkable 2024 campaign.

The next chapter of Gukesh's career will unfold against an opponent who is also young, ambitious and exceptionally talented. Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan has enjoyed a spectacular rise over the past year, winning the 2025 World Cup before dominating the Candidates Tournament in April 2026.

His qualification for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 sets the stage for a fascinating clash between two players representing the new generation of elite chess. Both have already demonstrated their ability to compete at the highest level, but they arrive at the match from very different positions. While Sindarov will be eager to seize his first opportunity to become world champion, Gukesh must prove that he can rediscover his championship-winning form and withstand the unique pressure of defending the crown.

The old saying goes that defending a title is often more difficult than winning it in the first place. For Gukesh, the challenge is arguably even greater: he must overcome not only a formidable opponent but also the recent struggles that have interrupted his progress.

In recent months, the Indian champion has reportedly sought time for reflection and preparation, with his visit to the Tirumala Temple in Andhra Pradesh in early November attracting attention. Whatever role such moments of introspection may play, there is little doubt that Gukesh will be determined to give himself every possible chance of success. There is no doubt that he possesses all the ingredients required to mount a successful title defence. His opening versatility, exceptional calculating ability, resilience under pressure and fearless approach to complicated positions remain major strengths. Above all, his ability to rise to the occasion has already been demonstrated on the biggest stages, from the Candidates Tournament to the final game of the 2024 World Championship match.

Photo: Michal Walusza

For Gukesh, the Geneva match will be about much more than retaining the world title. It will be an opportunity to reaffirm his place among the very best, silence doubts about his recent performances, and demonstrate that his historic triumph in Singapore was the beginning of a new era rather than the peak of a brief but extraordinary journey.

title: Bavarian Championship: Sasikiran joins Gopal in the lead
summary:
With 6 points from 7 rounds, Indian grandmasters Krishnan Sasikiran and G.N. Gopal share the lead at the Bavarian Chess Championship in Tegernsee. Their opponents' average ratings of 2413 (Sasikiran) and 2411 (Gopal) also leave them closely matched on tiebreaks, with both having faced stronger opposition on average than any other participant. Gopal drew with Elham Amar on the top board. While the games on the neighbouring boards also ended in draws, including Frederik Svane (5½/7) against Adrian Gschnitzer, Sasikiran secured a win over Rithvik Raja. | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Two co-leaders, two rounds to go

After round seven, the Bavarian Championship is led by the two Indian GMs, Krishnan Sasikiran and G.N. Gopal. Gopal was able to maintain his advantage over most of his direct pursuers, as the games on the first five boards all ended in draws, but Sasikiran scored a win against his compatriot Rithvik Raja and was able to move into shared first place. Sasikiran and Gopal are therefore both on 6 points and lead the standings.

Frederik Svane drew with black on board two against Adrian Gschnitzer. With 5½ points, Frederik Svane is only half a point behind the leaders before the penultimate round on Saturday. Leonardo Costa drew with Roven Vogel, while Alexander Donchenko defeated Moritz Weishaeutel to join Frederik Svane and Leonardo Costa. In total, 21 players are on 5½ points.

The two highest-placed women are Maria Tsakona (47 th ) and Kateryna Dolzhykova (49 th ), both on 5 points.

Adrian Gschnitzer and Frederik Svane | Photo: Sandra Schmidt

Adrian Gschnitzer v. Frederik Svane

In his game against Frederik Svane, Adrian Gschnitzer managed to obtain an advantage. In the endgame, he captured a pawn with check, and it was precisely this move that gave Frederik Svane the opportunity to get back into the game and hold the draw.

At this point, there was already a material imbalance. Gschnitzer had a rook, bishop and five pawns, while Svane had two rooks and three pawns. After 45.Bxe5+ Kg8 46.Bf6 Rxe4+ , Black had enough activity with his rooks to win or exchange all but two of White's pawns. In the end, they agreed to a draw.

In this endgame, Frederik Svane showed plenty of patience and held out in a complicated position long enough to reach an equal position again. In the final position, he could still have captured the b-pawn, but neither side could see a way to win.

title: 100-0 Denied: Bullet Grandpa Beats Dubov In Game 28
summary:
Arizona businessman and amateur chess player Josh Smith (@BulletGrandpa) won a single game against super-GM Daniil Dubov in the final match of the 100-0 Project Season 1 to prevent a super-adoption. The question was whether a super-grandmaster can beat an amateur in 100 consecutive bullet games without a single draw. Smith won game 28, though Dubov won all 99 of the other games.

Dubov earned $10,000 for participating, but not the $20,000 promised for winning the match. IM Danny Rensch also announced Season 2 will take place from December 2026 to March 2027, culminating in a match against final boss GM Levon Aronian.

Greg Mustreader and Smith created the 100-0 Project to pit an amateur bullet enthusiast against world-class opposition in a match that can, in theory, go either way. "Can the absolute best players in the world beat me 100-0?" asked the Bullet Grandpa, who is 49 years old, in the video trailer. The answer, at least in the first edition, is no.

Smith had prepared for months ahead of the final boss, Dubov. From September through October, he played 50-game matches against many content creators and chess personalities. As you can see in the table below, he wasn't swept in any of them, even by GMs Arturs Neiksans or Vasif Durarbayli.

While the training matches consisted of 50 games, the final match was 100. The time control was 1+0, the standard for "pure" bullet.

On October 6, Bullet Grandpa—who estimates he's played over 250,000 bullet games—had set his record of 2579 rating in bullet chess, but he started this match with a 2424 rating. Dubov was at a monstrous 3225. The grandmaster won the first 27 games with several sacrifices and brilliant moves along the way.

Dubov's vast opening knowledge, even of dubious lines, was on full display in this match—and even with just a minute, he converted advantages with brutal precision. Game three was a good example of Dubov winning right out of the opening against a Czech Benoni. After 9.Bb5+, there's no good move to recommend for Black. He fell apart.

The first nine games were all one-sided. Game six was a 16-move miniature that Dubov won with the black pieces. The attack started with the pawn sacrifice 7...e3! to open up the white king.

Efficiency is key in bullet chess, as you want to win quickly to avoid even the possibility of losing on time. Dubov hardly got into time trouble, and 40.f3 in the next game is a good example of Dubov's incisive conversion. The game ended with a satisfying checkmate just one move later.

Game 10 is the closest Smith got to holding a draw in the early stage, but trading into the knight endgame allowed Dubov to take over in an equal-material endgame with the more active king.

One of the biggest fears for Dubov must have been a mouse slip. We did see a mouse slip in game 14, but as GM Kayden Troff (Smith's coach) announced, "The first mouse slip, but not for Dubov!"

In game 15, Dubov's queen sacrifice 27.Qc6!! is one of the best moves of the day. If the queen is captured, 28.Rb8 is checkmate.

In game 24, Smith outplayed Dubov briefly but went on to lose control in the rook and opposite-color bishop endgame. The grandmaster went on to win with a rare checkmate, strangely ending the game with a king move!

Every 25 games, the players took a break. So three games after the first break, Smith had already decided the match. In game 28, Smith hung his queen, Dubov didn't see it and hung his bishop in return, and the amateur went on to win in the time scramble.

Josh Smith hangs his queen, but Dubov doesn't see it and blunders a bishop in return! Smith is now winning! https://t.co/BPb9w8FO0t https://t.co/EH6re6YTAQ

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Celebrating the victory, Bullet Grandpa yelled out, "He's human!"

"He's human! He bleeds!" The Bullet Grandpa celebrates as he wins game 28, so Dubov is unable to win 100-0! https://t.co/MpFf1h5pdS

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Although the experiment was effectively over, the players continued the match and played out the rest of the games. The lowered stakes may have helped Dubov loosen up, and he surprised even himself with the 99-1 final score. He said he expected 97-3 or even 95-5. "There were two or three games where I was lucky chess-wise," he said, referring to games he saved on time rather than by the strength of his moves. The following clip shows one of those games:

The Bullet Grandpa nearly wins a second game, but Dubov slips away and wins! https://t.co/Ros1zuiN6d

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2026

Smith, after denying the sweep, said, "I was just blown away. I've never played a super-elite player of Dubov's caliber before, and I have incredible respect for his tactics." He said the match was even more difficult than he thought it would be. And he explained: "I run out of ideas. I run out of moves, and it feels so hopeless, but I try to come up with certain things, but it's so easy to put you up on a pedestal and say that you're [Dubov] just inhuman, that you're just a robot."

I was just blown away. I've never played a super-elite player of Dubov's caliber before.

—Josh Smith

Dubov responded, "It's not about a pedestal or whatever. It's just you've gotta wait for this blunder, and this blunder will come for sure. And there will be like five games where you get a chance, or maybe more games actually."

You've gotta wait for this blunder, and this blunder will come for sure. And there will be like five games where you get a chance, or maybe more games actually.

—Daniil Dubov's advice for Smith

As the Bullet Grandpa prepares for Season 2, which will feature a final match against Aronian, he will have to think hard about his openings with White. Dubov explained he'd watched some of the training matches and recommended playing those in secret next time. He identified a pattern: Smith likes to play, regardless of move orders, the moves d4, Nf3, b3, Bb2, g3, Bg2—that kind of setup, which you can easily premove. Dubov trusted he'd get better positions with White every game, but he did work on countering this setup with Black.

Can the Bullet Grandpa do it again, against Levon Aronian? Let us know your Season 2 predictions in the comments below!

How to review?

You can review the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages. You can also check out The Bullet Grandpa on YouTube.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM Kayden Troff and Greg Mustreader.

An amateur bullet enthusiast from Arizona took on a gauntlet of streamers and masters in epic matches, all building toward one shot at super-GM Daniil Dubov. The final match, taking place on November 7 on Chess.com, was a 100-game match with a 1+0 time control per game. Winning all 100 games would have earned Dubov the full $20,000 prize, while a single draw for the Bullet Grandpa would have resulted in Dubov earning just $10,000.

title: Janak Awatramani Wins His 2nd Crazyhouse Championship
summary:
NM Janak Awatramani beat GM Guillermo Vazquez 3-0 in the Grand Final to win the 2026 Crazyhouse Championship, following up on his victory in 2024. Crazyhouse, as commentator GM Yasser Seirawan mentioned, is often called "Bughouse for one player," so it's perhaps no surprise that Awatramani has won the last two Bughouse championships as well. He did that together with NM Isaac Chiu, who took the Crazyhouse title in 2025, but this time Awatramani won their Winners Final clash 3-1.

The next Chess.com Community Championship, on December 17-18, is the 2026 Fog Of War Championship.

Final Bracket

What Is Crazyhouse?

Qualifiers: Awonder Liang Drops Out

Knockout: Awatramani Storms To Title

What Is Crazyhouse?

Crazyhouse follows the same pattern as Bughouse in that captured pieces can return to the board, but it's a game for two players instead of four. Rather than passing a piece to your partner, you can choose to place it on the board yourself instead of moving another piece. Here are the rules that differ from normal chess.

When you capture an opponent's piece, it is placed in your "pool" of pieces, and you can "drop" it on an empty square on your turn.

Pieces may only be dropped on empty squares.

You may drop a piece to give check or checkmate.

Pawns may not be dropped on the first or eighth ranks.

It follows that you can get unusual piece arrangements, such as a four-bishop defensive setup!

The value of the initiative is huge, since an attack fuels itself as you capture and re-add pieces. There are essentially no endgames—since pieces return to the board—and draws are rare, but they can be amusing when they do occur! (This one is from 2025.)

Draws are rare in Crazyhouse, but Yasser explains how you make them! pic.twitter.com/g5VDTo7LuT

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 7, 2025

The Chess.com Crazyhouse Championship featured eight arena qualifiers followed by an eight-player final tournament.

Qualifiers: Awonder Liang Drops Out

Thursday saw eight qualifiers, which players of all levels could register for. They were 75-minute arenas with a 3+0 time control and produced the following eight qualifiers, including three Canadians.

The highest winning score was 123 points for IM Mark Plotkin, who once went on a 19-game winning streak. The lowest winning score was 60 points, for Justin Tan, but that was also one of the most welcome qualifications. "JannLee" is a Crazyhouse legend who has won previous Chess.com Championships and is often considered the "first world champion" of the game.

Some top players missed out, including GM Jeffery Xiong, who was second to Chiu in the first qualifier, and Seirawan, who twice finished fifth. That loss was the audience's gain, since he once again teamed up with GM Benjamin Bok to provide commentary.

The one disappointment is that GM Awonder Liang, the winner of the preceding Seirawan Chess Championship, qualified as the winner of the fourth arena but then was unable to play in the Finals. His spot would have gone to second-placed Vazquez, but as the Paraguayan GM won the next arena, it went to third-placed Brendan Cater instead.

Knockout: Awatramani Storms To Title

Three players won 3-0 in the opening matches of the Quarterfinals, but the remaining match was a thriller. Tan got off to a powerful start, taking a 2-0 lead against Chiu. The defending champion fought back, however, winning the next two games.

The second of those saw him dominate on the clock, but also finish off with checkmate on the board. There was only one good way to react to a pawn being dropped on h2, and Tan didn't find it.

Defending Crazyhouse Champion Isaac Chiu fights back from 2-0 down to force a decider! https://t.co/pjuZb8MBxM https://t.co/zVQ2fChGvM

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 6, 2026

Chiu went on to win the bullet decider convincingly, but Tan got to fight on in the Losers bracket.

He beat Cater 3-0 and then was only stopped 3-2 by FM Roee Aroesti (Crazy_Eight) in the Losers Quarterfinals. That finished in dramatic fashion, as Tan was down on time in the bullet decider but had mate-in-two on the board.

Down to under two seconds, Tan went astray here, but he could have grabbed the bishop on d4 with check and then dropped that bishop on a4 with checkmate next move!

Aroesti is the player who gave the eventual winner his toughest match, with Awatramani losing the first game of the Winners Semifinals from a completely winning position. He had to put a piece on f3—preventing Black from doing the same—and when he grabbed a rook on c8 instead, disaster followed. It's amazing how fast things can turn around in Crazyhouse.

Awatramani hit back to win the next two games, then lost again, but won in bullet with the white pieces.

That set up a Winners Final against his Bughouse partner Chiu, with Awatramani scoring an impressive 3-1 victory, though Chiu's win was perhaps the most memorable game of the match. Black's four rooks should have been more than enough to win, but one mistake led to a nice smothered mate.

So Awatramani was in the Grand Final, but who would he face? In the end, it came down to a hard-fought battle between Chiu and Vazquez. Vazquez took the lead twice, the second time in the most dramatic fashion possible—Chiu had mate-in-five in the final position, but didn't manage to make a move in 0.9 seconds against his opponent's single second.

Chiu hit back both times, however, and lost only in the bullet decider.

That meant a potentially thrilling final battle between the one grandmaster in the field, Vazquez, and Awatramani. In the end, however, it was anticlimactic—Awatramani blew his opponent away in 19 moves in game one, then was on top for almost all of game two before delivering mate-in-four.

The final must-win game for Vazquez had some swings, but Awatramani had the advantage for most of the encounter and finished things off nicely in a demonstration of how the material that's on the board in Crazyhouse can be very deceptive.

Congratulations to Canadian NM Janak Awatramani on clinching victory in the Crazyhouse Championship with a 3-0 win in the Grand Final! 🏆 https://t.co/tCpUQzXk82

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 6, 2026

Awatramani picked up the $750 top prize, with the top three also gifted a special set of 3D-printed Crazyhouse pieces (flip them to change their color) from our very own NM Sam Copeland.

There's now just one Community Championship left before the end of the year—the 2026 Fog Of War Championship on December 17-18. Once again, it's open to everyone, so don't miss out!

How to review?

You can review the 2026 Chess.com Community Championships: Crazyhouse on the Chess.com Twitch or YouTube pages.

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Yasser Seirawan and Benjamin Bok.

The 2026 Crazyhouse Chess Championship is the 11th event of the 2026 Chess.com Community Championship series. Winners of eight qualifiers (each was a 75-minute arena with a 3+0 time control) entered the Final on November 6, which was an eight-player double-elimination bracket. The time control was 3+0, and matches were best-of-four. The total prize fund was $2,500.
